feed.note: Relative download URLs beginning with ./ are resolved against this file and are used for local testing. Production entries use absolute https URLs.
feed.updates: Each app has its own GitHub repository and its own releases, so shipping a fix to one never means re-releasing the others. Set provider to github and fill in owner/repo to go live; provider local pins the app to the release recorded here.

apps.name: Ferry
apps.tagline: Copy large amounts of data and know for certain it arrived intact.
description: Windows Explorer copies files and tells you nothing about whether they survived the trip. Ferry hashes every file as it reads and re-reads the destination afterwards, so a completed transfer is a verified transfer rather than an assumed one.
Built for the cases Explorer handles badly: tens of thousands of small files, flaky external drives, and transfers that die three hours in.
features: Per-file hash verification, with a report of anything that failed
Files land as .ferrypart and only move into place once verified
Overwrite, skip, rename, or fail — applied in bulk rather than per file
Cancel without leaving a truncated file that looks complete
Honest progress: the whole transfer is measured before a byte moves

apps.name: Capture
apps.tagline: Screen capture and annotation without an annual bill.
description: Snagit retired its perpetual licence in 2026 and moved to subscription only. Capture does the part almost everyone actually used: take a region, a window, or a scrolling page, mark it up, and get it into a document.
The annotation layer stays editable. Arrows, boxes, step numbers, and redaction blocks remain objects you can move or delete until you flatten the image yourself.
features: Region, window, full screen, and scrolling capture
Editable annotation objects rather than baked-in pixels
Redaction that removes the underlying pixels, not a box drawn over them
Copy straight to clipboard, or save as PNG, JPG, or WebP
Capture history, so a shot taken twenty minutes ago is still recoverable

apps.name: Sheaf
apps.tagline: A full PDF editor — text, drawing, custom fonts, and images — entirely on your own machine.
description: The free web PDF tools all require uploading the document to somebody else's server, which rules them out for anything confidential. Sheaf does the same operations locally and nothing ever leaves the computer.

Beyond page rearrangement, Sheaf edits text already on the page in its own embedded font, and adds markup, freehand drawing, brand-new typed text in any font installed on your system, and images — all built from a from-scratch PDF engine, not a wrapper around someone else's library.
features: Merge, split, reorder, rotate, and extract from a visual page grid
Edit existing text in place, using the page's own embedded font
Highlight, underline, strikethrough, shapes, freehand ink, and sticky notes
Type new text in any font installed on your system — not a small bundled set
Insert images, redact text for real, remove known passwords, and compress embedded images
No upload, no account, no network access at all

apps.name: Compare
apps.tagline: Diff and merge files and whole folder trees.
description: Beyond Compare is excellent and fairly priced, which makes it a hard target. Compare aims at the eighty percent people actually use: side-by-side text diff, folder synchronisation, and knowing which of two directories is ahead.
Free alternatives exist, but most have not been redesigned in fifteen years.
features: Side-by-side text diff with word-level highlighting
Three-way merge with a clear resolution pane
Folder comparison by content hash, not just timestamp and size
One-way and mirrored sync, with a dry run before anything moves
Binary comparison with a hex view

apps.name: Expand
apps.tagline: Type a short trigger, get a long block of text.
description: Text expansion is a small idea that saves a surprising amount of time, and the established tools charge a lot for it. Expand watches for triggers you define and replaces them inline in any application.
Snippets support placeholders, so a template can stop and ask for the two or three values that change each time.
features: Inline expansion in any application that takes keyboard input
Placeholders that prompt for values before inserting
Date, time, and clipboard tokens computed at expansion time
Per-application scoping so triggers do not collide
Plain-file snippet storage you can back up yourself

apps.name: Batch
apps.tagline: Convert, resize, and watermark thousands of images at once.
description: Bulk image work is the kind of task people do once a month and pay for reluctantly. Batch builds a pipeline of operations, shows you exactly what it would write, then runs it across an entire folder tree.
Non-destructive is enforced rather than promised: it refuses to run if the output folder is also a source folder, and it refuses to run if two images would resolve to the same output name.
features: Chain resize, convert, watermark, and metadata stripping into one ordered pass
Reorder steps, because resizing before watermarking is not the same as after
Live preview of the resolved output names before anything is written
Name templates with {name} {n} {n:000} {width} {height} {date}
Metadata stripping, for images headed somewhere public
One unreadable file is reported and skipped, not fatal to the run

apps.name: Clip
apps.tagline: Clipboard history that is actually searchable.
description: Windows has a built-in clipboard history behind Win+V, and it is thin: no search worth the name, a short memory, and awkward handling of anything that is not plain text.
Clip keeps a longer history, indexes it for full-text search, and lets you pin the handful of things you paste constantly.
features: Full-text search across clipboard history
Pinned entries that survive restarts
Text, image, and file-list entries all retained
Automatic exclusion rules for password managers
Local encrypted store with a configurable retention window

apps.name: Purge
apps.tagline: Uninstall software and remove what it leaves behind.
apps.requirements: Windows 10 1809 or later, x64. Administrator rights required.
description: Windows uninstallers routinely leave registry keys, configuration folders, and scheduled tasks behind. Purge watches an uninstall, then scans for the leftovers and shows you what it found.
Nothing is deleted without review. The scan produces a list, you decide, and a restore point is written first.
features: Post-uninstall scan for orphaned keys, folders, and scheduled tasks
Every deletion reviewed before it happens
System restore point created automatically beforehand
Batch uninstall of several programs in one queue
Full log of everything removed, with an undo file

apps.name: Corral
apps.tagline: Group desktop icons into labelled areas that stay put.
description: Fences has been the answer to a messy desktop for years and has almost no credible free competition. Corral draws labelled, movable containers on the desktop and keeps icons inside them.
Layouts survive resolution changes and monitor reconfiguration, which is the specific thing that makes homegrown attempts fall apart.
features: Labelled containers that icons snap into and stay in
Roll a container up to its title bar to reclaim space
Layouts saved per display configuration
Rules that file new icons automatically by type or source
Double-click the desktop to hide every icon at once

apps.name: Span
apps.tagline: Window management and taskbars across multiple monitors.
description: PowerToys FancyZones covers window snapping for free and covers it well. Span targets what it leaves out: per-monitor taskbars, saved window layouts, and per-display wallpaper.
The aim is the multi-monitor gaps in Windows itself rather than a second attempt at zone snapping.
features: A taskbar on every monitor showing only that monitor's windows
Named window layouts, restored on demand or at login
Per-monitor wallpaper, including one image spanning all displays
Hotkeys to throw the focused window to the next display
Layout profiles that follow docking and undocking
